title: The Economics of Algorithmic Personalization: Evidence from an Educational Technology Platform
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether algorithmic personalization can improve engagement in educational technology, and whether effects found in an experiment persist or change when the algorithm is deployed at scale. The authors focus on the Freadom English-learning app in India, where low retention and limited engagement are central challenges for children’s reading practice. The study is especially concerned with whether recommendation systems developed for large entertainment platforms can work in a moderate-scale educational app and whether scaled algorithmic interventions show the usual “voltage drop” seen in policy scale-ups.

The intervention is a collaborative-filtering recommendation system that personalizes story recommendations based on users’ prior interactions. Freadom previously relied on editorially curated recommendations. The authors set an eligibility threshold of 60 prior story interactions, both because prediction accuracy improved after that point and because the threshold enabled a regression discontinuity design during scaled deployment. They first ran a randomized controlled trial with 7,750 eligible users for two weeks, assigning treatment users to personalized recommendations in the Recommended Story section while control users continued receiving editorial recommendations. They then studied five months of scaled deployment using the 60-interaction threshold as a regression discontinuity.

The population was Indian children aged 3–12 using Freadom to learn to read in English. Users accessed the app through school partnerships, parent downloads, and paid subscriptions. Outcomes were based on objective app-log measures of engagement, including story engagement, stories completed, reading time, and completion of more difficult stories; the study did not directly measure learning outcomes such as test scores.

The RCT found that personalization increased engagement in the personalized section by about 60% and app-wide engagement by about 14%, suggesting that users increased overall app use rather than merely shifting time away from other sections. During scaled deployment, regression discontinuity estimates were larger than the RCT benchmark, suggesting that algorithmic interventions may improve with scale as more data accumulate. However, benefits were front-loaded and diminished as users exhausted the best-matched stories, indicating that limited content inventory can become a binding constraint on sustained personalization gains.

identified_tools.name: Freadom
identified_tools.description: Freadom is a mobile and web English-learning application for children; in this study it incorporated a custom collaborative-filtering recommendation system to personalize story recommendations.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studied personalized story recommendations for Indian children aged 3–12 learning English. Users with at least 60 prior story interactions received collaborative-filtering recommendations in Freadom’s Recommended Story section, compared with editorial curation in an RCT and then evaluated during scaled deployment using an eligibility-threshold RDD.

findings.finding_summary: In the randomized controlled trial, personalized recommendations increased app-wide Total Story Engagement by ATE=0.522, equal to 13.767% of the control mean, with SE=0.27. The paper reports 7,750 randomized users, and Table 5 reports 1,376 treated observations and 1,430 control observations for this outcome.
findings.measure: Total Story Engagement across all app sections
findings.sample_size: n=7,750 randomized; Table 5: treated n=1,376, control n=1,430

findings.finding_summary: Personalized recommendations increased app-wide Stories Completed by ATE=0.359, equal to 18.979% of the control mean, with SE=0.16. The effect was statistically significant at p<0.05 in Table 5.
findings.measure: Stories completed across all app sections
findings.sample_size: n=7,750 randomized; Table 5: treated n=1,376, control n=1,430

findings.finding_summary: Within the Recommended Story section where personalization was deployed, personalized recommendations increased Total Story Engagement by ATE=0.171, equal to 60.265% of the control mean, with SE=0.052. The effect was statistically significant at p<0.01 in Table 5.
findings.measure: Total Story Engagement in the Recommended Story section
findings.sample_size: n=7,750 randomized; Table 5: treated n=1,376, control n=1,430

findings.finding_summary: Within the Recommended Story section, personalized recommendations increased Stories Completed by ATE=0.119, equal to 77.478% of the control mean, with SE=0.037. The effect was statistically significant at p<0.01 in Table 5.
findings.measure: Stories completed in the Recommended Story section
findings.sample_size: n=7,750 randomized; Table 5: treated n=1,376, control n=1,430

findings.finding_summary: Personalized recommendations increased app-wide Total Reading Time by ATE=2.501, equal to 19.781% of the control mean, with SE=1.104. The paper interprets this as evidence that engagement gains also increased a learning-related input rather than merely shifting users to easier or shorter content.
findings.measure: Total Reading Time across all app sections
findings.sample_size: n=7,750 randomized; Table 6: treated n=1,376, control n=1,430

findings.finding_summary: Personalized recommendations increased the Number of Difficult Stories completed app-wide by ATE=0.369, equal to 19.713% of the control mean, with SE=0.16. Difficult stories were defined as stories whose assigned grade level exceeded the user’s grade level.
findings.measure: Number of Difficult Stories completed across all app sections
findings.sample_size: n=7,750 randomized; Table 6: treated n=1,376, control n=1,430

findings.finding_summary: During five months of scaled deployment, regression discontinuity estimates for users around the 60-interaction eligibility threshold exceeded the RCT benchmark by a factor of 2.5, with p<0.001. The paper reports that gains were front-loaded, concentrated in users’ first weeks of exposure, and diminished thereafter as high-quality content matches were exhausted.
findings.measure: User engagement during scaled deployment, estimated using the 60-interaction eligibility-threshold regression discontinuity design
findings.effect_size: RDD estimates exceeded RCT benchmark by a factor of 2.5; p<0.001

quality_tier_rationale: The paper reports a large randomized controlled trial plus a regression discontinuity design during scaled deployment, with validation checks and pre-registration noted. Some caution remains because the main outcomes are behavioral engagement measures, and the analysis sample reported for active users differs from the full randomized sample.
impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced positive engagement effects, including a 14% app-wide increase in Total Story Engagement and a 60% increase within the personalized section in the RCT. Impact is not rated blue because the paper explicitly measures engagement and learning inputs rather than direct learning outcomes such as test scores.
